function.name: generate_report
function.description: Generates a comprehensive report based on user activity data within a specified time frame. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

user_id.description: The unique identifier for the user.

start_date.description: The start date for the report period in the format 'YYYY-MM-DD'.

end_date.description: The end date for the report period, inclusive, in the format 'YYYY-MM-DD'.

include_inactive.description: Flag to determine if inactive users should be included in the report.

report_format.description: The format in which the report will be generated.

**Ionisation methods – a quick guide** | Ionisation technique | Typical application | Key advantages | Common limitations | |----------------------|---------------------|----------------|--------------------| | **Electron Impact (EI)** | Gas‑phase mass spectrometry (GC‑MS) | • Produces reproducible, highly fragmentary spectra
• Good for small, volatile molecules | • Requires vacuum and a gas‑phase sample
• Not suitable for large biomolecules | | **Chemical Ionisation (CI)** | GC‑MS, LC‑MS | • Softer than EI → less fragmentation
• Useful for thermally labile compounds | • Still requires gas‑phase sample
• Lower sensitivity for some analytes | | **Photoionisation (PI)** | GC‑MS, LC‑MS | • Non‑destructive, minimal fragmentation
• Can be tuned with different photon energies | • Requires UV source; limited to UV‑absorbing compounds | | **Electrospray Ionisation (ESI)** | LC‑MS, proteomics, metabolomics | • Soft, produces multiply charged ions → high‑molecular‑weight analytes
• Works directly from solution | • Suppression effects in complex matrices
• Requires careful tuning of solvent & flow | | **Matrix‑Assisted Laser Desorption/Ionisation (MALDI)** | Proteomics, polymers, large biomolecules | • Very soft, minimal fragmentation
• High throughput, can analyze solids | • Requires matrix preparation
• Less quantitative | | **Atmospheric Pressure Chemical Ionisation (APCI)** | LC‑MS, small molecules | • Good for moderately polar compounds
• Works with high‑flow LC | • Less effective for very polar or large molecules | | **Atmospheric Pressure Photoionisation (APPI)** | LC‑MS, non‑polar compounds | • Extends MS to non‑polar analytes
• Soft ionisation | • Requires a UV lamp; not as common | | **Laser Ablation Ionisation (LAI)** | Surface analysis, solid samples | • Direct sampling of solids
• Minimal sample prep | • Requires laser system; can cause fragmentation | | **Field Ionisation (FI)** | Surface analysis, small molecules | • Very soft, minimal fragmentation | • Requires high electric fields; limited throughput | ### How to choose the “best” method 1. **Sample type & state** * Gas‑phase → EI, CI, PI. * Liquid or aqueous → ESI, APCI, APPI. * Solid or surface → MALDI, LAI, FI. 2. **Molecular weight & polarity** * Small, volatile, non‑polar → EI, CI. * Large, polar, biomolecules → ESI, MALDI. * Non‑polar, high‑MW → APPI. 3. **Desired information** * Structural elucidation (fragmentation) → EI, CI, PI. * Quantitation & high‑throughput → ESI, MALDI. * Minimal fragmentation (intact mass) → MALDI, APPI. 4. **Instrumentation & cost** * EI/CI/PI require a GC‑MS system. * ESI/APCI/APPI need LC‑MS. * MALDI needs a MALDI‑TOF or MALDI‑MS instrument. 5. **Matrix effects & sensitivity** * ESI is prone to ion suppression in complex matrices; use cleanup or alternative ionisation. * MALDI can suffer from uneven matrix crystallisation; careful sample prep helps. --- #### Bottom line - **For routine GC‑MS of small, volatile compounds:** *Electron Impact* is the gold standard. - **For large biomolecules (proteins, peptides):** *Electrospray* (ESI) or *MALDI* are the go‑to methods. - **For non‑polar, high‑MW analytes in LC‑MS:** *APPI* offers a soft, efficient alternative. - **For surface or solid‑state analysis:** *Laser Ablation* or *Field Ionisation* can be considered. If you have a specific sample type or analytical goal in mind, let me know and I can narrow down the recommendation further!
